articles.title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' sales would astonish the 'godfather of video games' if it hit this number
articles.summary: GTA 6 is coming, and it has big sales goals to hit.
articles.body:
"Grand Theft Auto VI" from Take-Two Interactive ( TTWO ) has a shot at blowing the minds of investors amid intense anticipation for the game's release in a few weeks.

"Success looks like if 10% of the people who watch the preview video — I think it was something like 750 million people — if they go out and buy the game, that would be mind-blowing," Electronic Arts co-founder and Kleiner Perkins partner Bing Gordon said on Sozzi Unleashed .

Gordon — known in gaming circles as the "godfather of video games" for his work on popular properties such as "Madden" — sits on the board of directors of Take-Two Interactive.

Take-Two Interactive has been led by CEO Strauss Zelnick for about 15 years.

"You know, the movie business still brags about a $300 million box office, and a $1 billion box office blows their minds. The games business has been bigger than the movie business for a long period of time, first in hours and then in money. So you always want to be the best ever." Gordon added. "I think from my point of view, what success for GTA 6 is going to be on Thanksgiving Day after eating your turkey, you don't watch football, you play GTA."

For Take-Two Interactive, the release of "Grand Theft Auto VI" represents not just a flagship title but a transformative financial catalyst.

Keep in mind that "Grand Theft Auto V," released some 10 years ago, has generated nearly $8 billion in lifetime retail revenue and sold more than 200 million units, with the game continuing to be upgraded for online players.

"Grand Theft Auto VI" launches on Nov. 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S at $79.99. Buyers of digital preorders can start preloading the game on Nov. 12.

Experts have pegged opening-week sales projections reaching up to $4.5 billion. GTA 6 is expected to be so hot that it will pull users away from other games in droves — including those on Roblox ( RBLX ).

Somewhat oddly, despite the excitement around "Grand Theft Auto VI," Take-Two Interactive stock is down 12% in the past three months compared to a 4% advance for the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ).

"We would be buyers of TTWO shares at $200, near year to date-lows and 20x P/E," Jefferies analyst James Heaney said. articles.body:
Boeing ( BA ) finally gave Wall Street a quarter with more free cash flow than expected. Investors dumped the stock anyway, because the company still can't get its planes out the door fast enough.

Boeing ( BA ) stock fell nearly 11% Tuesday, its worst day since June 2020, and closed at its lowest level since April 2025. It hit a new 52-week low on more than four times its usual volume and is now down more than a fifth this year. (For more on the quarter, see our earnings live blog .)

The third quarter itself was mixed. Revenue of about $24 billion and free cash flow of $464 million both topped Bloomberg estimates. But the core loss of $0.34 per share was wider than the $0.21 analysts expected, and the commercial jet unit lost about $700 million, roughly twice the forecast.

That unit's sales "were in line, but margin came in [about] 280 bps light due to cost growth," JPMorgan analyst Seth Seifman wrote in a note. In other words, its profit margin came in almost 3 percentage points short.

The stock sell-off deepened as Boeing laid out its production plans on the earnings call. The 737 will stay at 47 jets per month into next year, with the step up to 52 not coming until the second half of 2027. Boeing now expects to fall about 500 short on its 737 deliveries this year, and engine supply is setting the pace for 787 output.

Demand isn't the issue. Boeing's backlog hit a record $745 billion, including more than 6,300 jets.

The commercial jet business has made money in just one of the past 18 quarters. Analysts still expect it to get close to break-even by early 2027, a goal that now rests on a slower ramp.

The stock has mostly traded between about $150 and $250 since 2020, with $210 as the first potential ceiling on any rebound.

Boeing's October delivery numbers, due next month, will show whether the 737 line is holding at 47 a month.

articles.title: Robinhood stock falls 7% after earnings miss despite record trading volumes
articles.summary: Robinhood stock slumped in extended trading after a Q3 earnings miss on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Robinhood ( HOOD ) reported a weaker-than-expected third quarter profit on Tuesday as declining interest income and rising expenses weighed on the online brokerage despite record trading activity in stocks, options, and prediction markets.

The company reported net income of $476 million, down 14% from a year earlier, while diluted earnings per share fell 16% to $0.51. Revenue rose 12% to $1.42 billion. Analysts had expected earnings of $0.57 per share and revenue of $1.43 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Robinhood stock fell 7% in after-hours trading. The stock has slumped more than 15% since the start of 2026 through Tuesday's close, putting it on pace for its worst annual performance since 2022.

This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.

The company's investing platform experienced record trading volumes across stocks, options, and prediction markets, spurring transaction revenue 19% higher from a year earlier to $867 million.

But that frenzy was offset by a 9% decline in net interest revenue to $415 million. Robinhood said the decline was driven in part by lower securities lending activity.

Robinhood CFO Shiv Verma said weaker demand to borrow stocks weighed on the online brokerage's securities lending business, citing fewer IPOs and less disagreement among investors over the prospects of individual companies.

"Right now, there was lower market volatility, and there was less IPOs, and so there were lower requests for demand," Verma said on a call with reporters.

"The core business is on fire," he added.

Still, Robinhood's operating expenses also climbed 16% to $739 million while provisions for credit losses nearly tripled to $71 million as Robinhood expanded its credit card business. The company also reported $67 million in unrealized investment losses, primarily from its venture fund.

Excluding certain items, adjusted net income fell 3% to $550 million.

Robinhood attracted $15.7 billion in net deposits during the quarter, compared with $21.7 billion in the previous quarter. CFO Verma, however, added that the company disclosed deposits already surpassed $13 billion, driven in part by the Dell family's contribution to Trump Accounts .

Prediction markets remained an important growth driver. Revenue from event contracts surged to $173 million, up 11% from the previous quarter , as customers traded a record 16.4 billion contracts during the quarter.

Options trading revenue rose 31% to $399 million from a year ago, while equities trading revenue increased 41% to $121 million over the same period. Meanwhile, crypto trading revenue plunged 55% to $120 million amid a slump in activity.

articles.title: Trump Casts High Gas Price as ‘Short-Term Pain’ at Texas Rally
articles.summary: President Donald Trump returned to Texas on Tuesday in a final attempt to boost Senate candidate Ken Paxton, whose close race in a normally reliable conserva...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump returned to Texas on Tuesday in a final attempt to boost Senate candidate Ken Paxton, whose close race in a normally reliable conservative-leaning state has Republicans worried about losing control of the chamber.

Trump sought to cast Democratic challenger James Talarico as too far left for voters and at the same time pleaded for patience over high energy prices, fueled in part by the war in Iran.

High prices that have strained household budgets have become the dominant issue in the election, weighing down Republican candidates in red states such as Texas.

Trump on Tuesday defended his decision to attack Iran, saying it was "one of the greatest things I ever did," and claiming that prices at the pump would fall once the war is over, even with no clear off-ramp to a conflict now in its eighth month.

"Short-term pain, right, for long-term gain. You're going to see very soon," Trump said at a rally in Corpus Christi.

The average price for a gallon of regular was $4.27, according to auto club AAA, up from $2.98 before the war.

The president also hailed an oil tanker arriving at the Corpus Christi port from Venezuela, an effort to showcase energy supplies from the Latin American country. He earlier told reporters he would visit the ship.

The Trump administration has touted its control over Venezuela's natural resources after capturing former leader Nicolás Maduro.

Earlier: Trump, Rubio Plan to Visit Tanker With Venezuelan Crude in Texas

"It'll be refined right here in Texas, including right here in Corpus Christi," Trump said at the rally. "And you'll see, it'll happen very quickly. It'll be like a blink. Gasoline and diesel prices will soon come down."

In an effort to mobilize conservative voters in Texas, the president also repeated his attacks on Talarico, including accusations that he is a vegan, opposes gun rights, and supports transgender individuals.

"The only man standing between Texas and this raging lunatic is a man named President Donald J. Trump," Trump said. "And I need the help of Ken Paxton."

With Democrats needing to net only four seats to take control of the Senate, the race in Texas has taken on outsized importance and given them hope of achieving a long-sought goal of turning the state blue.

articles.title: The Fed says it ignores politics. Its rate moves tell a more complicated story
articles.summary: Independence from elected officials isn’t just something Federal Reserve officials preach – it’s engrained in the central bank’s bylaws.
articles.body: Federal Reserve officials agree that inflation needs to return to the central bank’s 2% annual target. Instead, the war with Iran has sent gas prices soaring, and price increases are starting to spread beyond the gas station. Last month, that prompted Fed officials to raise rates for the first time in three years to cool the economy and bring down inflation. Yet this month, even with the inflation picture worsening, the Fed is widely expected to hold rates steady at its Wednesday meeting. Would that still be the case if the midterms weren’t just six days away? At his 2:30 p.m. press conference Wednesday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is likely to face questions about political pressure if the central bank does keep rates unchanged. The Fed’s independence is a cornerstone of its monetary policy decisions. However, in an election year, that independence inevitably comes under the microscope. Outside of the pandemic, when rates were kept at near-zero levels, the Fed adjusted rates within two months of Election Day in four out of five of the most recent election years. In September 2024, for example, the Fed slashed its benchmark interest rate by half a point just six weeks before the presidential election. That marked the start of a cutting cycle as inflation cooled and officials grew concerned about a weakening labor market. Meanwhile, leading into the 2022 elections, the central bank pushed out two consecutive three-quarter point hikes, triple the size of the typical rate move, as it battled the worst inflation in almost four decades. And at the meeting after Election Day it announced another hike, this time a smaller half point. In 2016, officials didn’t change rates at the two immediate meetings before Election Day and instead hiked rates by a quarter point at the subsequent meeting. At that time, then-Philadelphia Fed President Patrick Harker supported a rate hike in September. However, he said he was opposed to hiking at the November meeting that was just six days before the presidential election. “What I’m worried about is depending on the outcome of the election and what happens after that, if there are policies that would have distortive effects that we would have to respond to, we’ll have to respond,” Harker said in remarks in October 2016. “And I don’t know which way that will go. But it may be prudent to wait until we have resolved some of that uncertainty.” Then-Fed Chair Janet Yellen, though, said the election did not play any role in officials’ decision-making process. Leading up to this week’s meeting, Fed officials have signaled that they believe economic conditions don’t warrant another immediate hike and that they would rather wait for more data. That’s because raising rates too early could unnecessarily weaken the economy — for example, by prompting consumers to pull back on spending as borrowing costs rise. That measured approach contrasts with President Donald Trump’s demands for lower rates. Elected officials, particularly presidents, tend to favor lower interest rates because that makes it cheaper for consumers and businesses to borrow. Trump, whose support has been faltering in recent months as gas prices and other costs have risen, has increased his pressure on the Fed to lower rates. Trump tapped Warsh to succeed Fed Chair Jerome Powell after repeatedly criticizing the central bank for not aggressively cutting rates. But Warsh’s first major move as head of the central bank was a rate hike, a decision that many viewed as a sign he wasn’t going to let politics interfere with Fed policy. Nonetheless, if the Fed does hold rates steady as expected, Warsh may have to work harder than usual to convince Americans that the political calendar played no part in its decision. (While the Fed chair has considerable power at the Fed, the position represents just one vote on a 12-person committee.) “Tightening cannot appear to be a move against the administration, while holding cannot look like accommodation,” EY-Parthenon chief economist Gregory Daco said in a note last week. Meanwhile, Bank of America head of US economic research Aditya Bhave noted that since investors expect the Fed to hold rates steady, a hike could now catch markets off guard and trigger further volatility at an already tense time.

Obama’s Cheesecake Factory jab spurs a midterm spat

A Cheesecake Factory jab from former President Obama quickly spiraled into a midterm spat between the GOP and Democrats as the competitive election cycle nears its end.

© Damian Dovarganes, The Associated Press

Obama quipped during a recent campaign stop in Cleveland that President Trump has the White House “looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory, it’s just gold everywhere.”

His remarks referred to Trump’s reported $900 million renovations to the White House, including pricey updates to the Rose Garden and constructing a new granite helipad, according to The Washington Post. Hussein’s Iraqi palaces were also famously adorned with gold fixtures and decor.

“We have to explain to Obama that the White House is a symbol of America, and it has to be maintained properly ,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland en route to Mississippi on Monday.

“It has to be painted, and the exterior plaster can’t be falling off the walls, and the decorations and the ornaments on the windows that are magnificent can’t be on one side of the window and falling off on the other side,” he continued.

“It’s not about money. It’s about seeing. Guys like Obama don’t see it. He doesn’t see dirt, he doesn’t see filth, he doesn’t see broken ornaments on a building,” Trump fired back at the former president. “For you to say it was a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president.”

The White House’s account on social platform X also joined in, posting a doctored Cheesecake Factory menu touting Trump administration policies, including items labeled “The Border Security Special” and “The American Energy Feast.”

“Since we’re talking about The Cheesecake Factory,” it wrote. “The only thing bigger than the menu is the list of President Trump’s accomplishments.”

articles.title: Fed expected to hold interest rates steady as inflation tops midterm voters’ concerns
articles.summary: Officials believe there is plenty of time left to tackle inflation, allowing them to avoid making a move so close to an election.
articles.body: The Federal Reserve is meeting in Washington this week, when it will consider whether to raise interest rates in an effort to tamp down on inflation. The meetings come at a moment when rising prices are shaping large parts of the U.S. economy and inflation is set to play a key role in next Tuesday’s midterm elections. Yet members of the bank’s interest rate-setting committee are widely expected to keep benchmark rates steady this month. There are several reasons the Fed is unlikely to move on rates Wednesday. Most of them come down to a sense among top officials that the central bank shouldn’t rush into interest rate decisions — and that it definitely shouldn’t do so less than a week out from Election Day. “Inflation remains above our goal,” Michelle Bowman, the Fed’s vice chair for supervision, said Oct. 14. “We have some time to wait and see how financial conditions evolve before we take more action.” The Fed last raised rates by a quarter of a percentage point in September after a string of monthly inflation readings well above its target of 2% and no signs that prices were coming down anytime soon. “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said at the time. Inflation figures for September, released this month, underscored Warsh’s point, with the annual inflation rate rising to 3.7% from 3.4% the previous month. Some analysts believe Warsh and the Fed will be taking a risk if they vote to hold rates steady, given the trajectory of inflation. “The case for skipping [a rate hike in] October is not terribly compelling,” analysts at Deutsche Bank wrote. Fed officials, however, point to a core tenet of the dual mandate that Congress has assigned to the Fed, of promoting maximum employment while maintaining stable prices. Specifically the “stable” part, which underpins the Fed’s famously slow and deliberative approach. “I don’t feel urgent that ​we have to decide with a limited set of information,” San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said in a recent interview. “I think we have the ⁠time that we need.” Another guiding principle at the Fed that is most likely tipping expectations about Wednesday is its tradition of staying far away from politics. If the Fed were to raise rates just days before the midterms, it could, at best, risk looking like a politically motivated decision. At worst, it could influence people’s votes. “We could imagine that all else equal the Fed might prefer to stay out of the headlines for raising rates just ahead of a midterm election where affordability is the principal concern,” the Deutsche Bank analysts wrote. Voters have repeatedly told pollsters that rising prices, especially in the housing and energy sectors, are their primary concerns as they cast their ballots. With control of both the House and the Senate on the line in Tuesday’s election, voters are clear about whom they blame for the higher prices: President Donald Trump’s war in Iran and his global tariff regime. The most recent NBC News poll found Trump’s approval rating at 27% for his handling of the cost of living and just 29% for his handling of the war with Iran. Two-thirds of Americans said the soaring gas prices triggered by Trump’s Iran war were either a “very serious” or a “somewhat serious” problem. Likewise, more than half of respondents said current economic conditions had caused them to change what kinds of groceries they buy. All that adds up to a very difficult political environment for Trump’s fellow Republicans, who are struggling to balance their general support for him with how unpopular his policies have become with voters. Even the Trump administration, which normally maintains an upbeat view about the economy and inflation, sounded concerned after the most recent inflation reading earlier in the month. “This was a disappointing number,” said Kevin Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council. Asked by Fox Business hosts why voters had such negative views of the current economy despite higher spending, Hassett was unsure. “It’s a puzzle that we’re noodling about every day,” he said.

articles.title: Conflicts Around the World Continue. Economists Are Seeing High Inflation Lasting Into 2027 as Energy Costs Spread.
articles.summary: Economists surveyed by Reuters raised their inflation forecasts for next year in 31 of the 50 economies covered, including 15 of 21 developed economies.
articles.body:
High inflation is likely to persist across much of the global economy well into 2027, according to a new specialized poll, as rising energy costs threaten to fuel broader and more lasting price increases.

Economists surveyed by Reuters in October raised their inflation forecasts for next year in 31 of the 50 economies covered, including 15 of 21 developed economies. They also raised growth projections for 23 economies, suggesting that persistent inflation could coincide with stronger economic activity than previously expected.

The findings point to a shift from Reuters polls in April and July, which had painted a picture of high inflation accompanied by weaker growth. Investment in artificial intelligence and stronger-than-expected activity in several regions have helped support the economy, even as households continue to struggle with the cost of living.

That resilience is also contributing to concerns that price pressures could prove difficult to contain. "I am getting much more concerned about inflation again," Janet Henry, global chief economist at HSBC, told the outlet.

Henry said the longer the conflict in the Middle East continues and escalates, and the more price pressures spread, the greater the likelihood that inflation will remain elevated for longer.

Oil has been a major source of pressure. Crude prices have remained above $100 a barrel since October 7 and rose above $117 last week, reaching a six-month high. Prices have climbed more than 60% since the war with Iran began nearly eight months ago.

Seth Carpenter, global chief economist at Morgan Stanley, said in a note that higher energy prices continue to ripple through the global economy. He added that signs were beginning to emerge that energy costs were passing through to measures of core inflation, which generally exclude volatile food and energy prices.

Over the past three quarterly Reuters polls, economists have raised their median 2027 inflation forecasts by a cumulative 0.7 percentage points for Britain, 0.5 points for the eurozone and 0.2 points for the United States. The forecast rose by 0.4 points for India and 0.5 points for Brazil.

Most central banks have raised interest rates only a few times or have held them steady. Further increases could follow if inflation spreads more widely, potentially keeping borrowing costs higher for households and businesses.

A sell-off in global bond markets in recent months has already pushed yields higher, tightening financial conditions. Higher bond yields can influence the cost of borrowing across the economy.

articles.title: Anthropic se prepara para um dos maiores IPOs da história; veja ranking | G1
articles.standfirst: Lista reúne empresas como SpaceX e Saudi Aramco. A OpenAI também planeja estrear na bolsa.
articles.summary: Lista reúne empresas como SpaceX e Saudi Aramco. A OpenAI também planeja estrear na bolsa.
articles.body:
Logo da Anthropic em ilustração feita em junho de 2026. — Foto: Dado Ruvic/Reuters

A Anthropic, empresa de inteligência artificial responsável pelo chatbot Claude , divulgou na segunda-feira (26) um pedido para abrir seu capital nos Estados Unidos . A operação pode colocar a companhia entre as protagonistas de uma das maiores estreias já registradas no mercado de ações.

🔎 IPO é a sigla em inglês para oferta pública inicial de ações. Na prática, é o processo pelo qual uma empresa passa a ter seus papéis negociados na bolsa, permitindo que investidores comprem uma participação no negócio.

A expectativa é que o IPO da Anthropic esteja entre os maiores já realizados e tenha impacto relevante no mercado americano, influenciando desde a composição de índices das bolsas até o movimento de grandes investidores.

“Uma oferta pública inicial bem-sucedida da Anthropic poderá abrir ou fechar de vez o mercado de IPOs, mesmo já em 2027”, disse Matt Kennedy, estrategista sênior da Renaissance Capital, uma empresa especializada em pesquisas focadas em IPOs e ETFs.

Entre os maiores IPOs da história estão o da SpaceX , atual recordista, e o da Saudi Aramco, que ocupava o posto desde 2019. A OpenAI também planeja uma oferta que pode ficar entre as maiores já realizadas. (veja o ranking abaixo)

Alguns investidores atuais e potenciais avaliam a Anthropic em cerca de US$ 1,5 trilhão , abaixo dos cerca de US$ 2 trilhões estimados anteriormente.

A revisão ocorreu após a empresa divulgar alguns de seus dados financeiros em um evento recente para investidores.

Segundo a Reuters, a empresa de inteligência artificial busca levantar até US$ 100 bilhões com o IPO, em novembro.

No fim de maio, a Anthropic captou US$ 65 bilhões com investidores, em uma operação que avaliou a empresa em US$ 965 bilhões.

OpenAI afirma que a confiança e a privacidade são fundamentais para seus produtos — Foto: Getty Images

A OpenAI , criadora do ChatGPT , revelou em junho que havia apresentado de forma confidencial um pedido para abrir seu capital nos EUA.

A empresa, no entanto, não abrirá o capital em 2026. A afirmação foi feita em setembro pelo presidente-executivo, Sam Altman.

Na ocasião, ele citou preocupações com a segurança da inteligência artificial. Segundo Altman, essas questões tornam “inaceitável” até mesmo um risco de 10% de que a IA possa causar a extinção da humanidade até o final da década.

A OpenAI busca garantir o compromisso de investidores antes da esperada estreia da rival Anthropic na bolsa.

A captação, considerada excepcionalmente rápida, pode avaliar a criadora do ChatGPT em mais de US$ 1,4 trilhão, segundo a Reuters.

“Ainda não decidimos o momento; pode demorar um pouco, pois há coisas que queremos fazer e que provavelmente são mais fáceis como empresa privada. Mas é um conjunto complicado de 'trade-offs', e isso nos dá a opção de abrir o capital mais cedo, se essa acabar sendo a melhor opção”, afirmou a OpenAI em junho.

Musk, Spacex e Tesla — Foto: REUTERS/Evan Vucci e REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Ilustração

A SpaceX , fabricante de foguetes e satélites de Elon Musk , estreou na Nasdaq em junho e quebrou o recorde de maior IPO da história . A operação superou com folga a da petrolífera Saudi Aramco, que detinha o posto desde 2019.

A empresa levantou US$ 75 bilhões com a oferta, mais que o dobro do arrecadado pela Saudi Aramco.

A companhia de Musk também fugiu do modelo tradicional ao definir o preço das ações antes das reuniões com investidores que normalmente antecedem a estreia na bolsa, processo conhecido como “roadshow”.

As ações encerraram o primeiro dia de negociação a US$ 160,95, levando o valor de mercado da SpaceX a US$ 2,1 trilhões.

Desde então, os papéis perderam parte da força. Em 23 de outubro, fecharam a US$ 147,49, ainda 9,3% acima dos US$ 135 cobrados no IPO.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Government has identified around 120 products, including intermediates and capital goods, for domestic manufacturing push and to reduce
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Government has identified around 120 products, including intermediates and capital goods, for domestic manufacturing push and to reduce dependence on imports, with a separate plan for tunnel boring machines in the works after China imposed restrictions on their shipments.As part of the exercise, which is being driven by the department for promotion of industry and internal trade (DPIIT), the range of products includes chemicals such as acetic acid, pharmaceutical products and inputs, medical technology related items, machine tools, including some textile looms, construction equipment, cranes, products used in the aerospace sector as MROs (maintenance, repair and operations) are coming up in the country. Besides, the list also includes some consumer goods, including products that are part of the footwear value chain, persons familiar with the discussions told TOI.While discussions are currently underway with other govt agencies, three types of intervention are planned. One, short-term protection that will enable products, which are identified, to deal with competition from overseas, especially China, till supplies are diversified. A similar strategy had been adopted in the case of mobile phones in the initial years.The second set of measures will deal with cost disability through incentives that could be capital incentives or phased over a period and may be linked to turnover. Also, on the menu is the option to provide R&D assistance as some of the products need to be developed locally as technology is not available.Over the last six-to-eight years, govt has sought to provide support to companies, both domestic and international, across sectors ranging from pharma and electronics to semiconductors, solar power equipment and white goods to encourage local production. A large part of the money has flown through PLIs, along with two semiconductor missions as well as a scheme aimed at enhancing production of electronic components in the country as demand for inputs has soared after domestic manufacturing of phones took off. Support for R&D probably flows from the experience in battery production as companies that have begun “local production” are essentially importing cells from China and selling battery packs as the entire production chain and technology is controlled by companies across the border. A similar experience was seen in the case of solar panels.The plan flows from govt’s overall Atmanirbhar Bharat strategy, which has received renewed attention after the West Asia crisis, when several critical items were in short supply locally due to large import dependence. articles.title: Global stock markets rise as investors continue to bet on AI
articles.summary: Asian markets make gains, following strong showing for US tech stocks.
articles.body:
Global stock markets have climbed as investors continue to bet on bright prospects for the tech giants driving the AI boom.

In the United States, all three major stock indexes rose on Tuesday, led by the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite, which gained 1.18 percent.

The benchmark S&P 500 rose 0.6 percent, while the narrower Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.03 percent.

Five of the “Magnificent Seven” tech stocks rose, led by Tesla, up 4.04 percent.

Amazon gained 1.61 percent, while Apple and Alphabet gained 0.93 percent and 0.9 percent, respectively.

Nvidia, the world’s most valuable public company, rose almost 1 percent after announcing a $3bn investment in Meta’s equity offering.

Meta fell 1.64 percent, while Microsoft fell 0.24 percent.

Other big movers in tech included CoreWeave, Western Digital and Advanced Micro Devices, which gained 7.94 percent, 6.95 percent and 5.45 percent, respectively.

Asian stock markets followed Wall Street’s gains on Wednesday.

South Korea’s KOSPI led the pack, with the benchmark index closing up 6.63 percent.

The surge came as South Korea’s SK Hynix, one of the world’s top three memory chip makers, announced blockbuster third-quarter results, with operating profit soaring about 630 percent year-on-year to 83.33 trillion won ($62.4bn).

SK Hynix’s South Korea-listed shares soared 10.89 percent following the results.

In Japan, the benchmark Nikkei 225 ended the day up 1.08 percent, while the TAIEX in Taiwan climbed 2.04 percent.

In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index was up 0.33 percent shortly before market closing.

“A rally in a host of AI-related stocks including neocloud group CoreWeave, data storage specialist Western Digital and IT solutions provider Super Micro Computing implies that investors aren’t over the AI craze just yet,” Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell in London, told Al Jazeera.

“These types of stocks have become a litmus test for the mood of the market. They typically fall when investors are worried that the AI story might be running out of steam, and they rise when animal spirits are running high around the technological revolution,” Coatsworth said.

“The big unknown is whether this is the start of a new AI stock rally, or just a relief bounce after a period where investors were starting to question how long positive momentum could be sustained,” he added.

Investors are eagerly anticipating upcoming earnings reports from chief tech players as they try to gauge whether their huge investments in AI will pay dividends.

Microsoft and Alphabet report their latest results on Wednesday, followed by Amazon on Thursday and Apple on Monday.

On Monday, AI giant Anthropic filed paperwork for its hotly anticipated IPO, reporting a net loss of $80.7bn in the first half of 2026 on $16.3bn in revenue.

Tech firms have poured hundreds of billions of dollars each into AI infrastructure, prompting debate over whether a speculative market bubble could be forming similar to the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash.

Global AI investment is forecast to hit $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to Gartner, a technology insights company.

Oil prices, which have been elevated since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, rose nearly 2 percent percent amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, including hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis.

Futures for Brent crude, the global benchmark, topped $116 a barrel, up more than 60 percent from before the war began.

articles.title: Layoffs, rebranded: Corporate euphemisms meet the AI reset
articles.summary: Corporate layoffs get rebranded with new euphemisms as AI reshapes workforce plans; Microsoft’s “voluntary exit offer” signals ongoing job pressure.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Companies have never liked the word “fired”. It sounds too much like what actually happened. So every few years, corporate vocabulary comes to the rescue with a softer term for the same hard conversation.“Downsizing”, “rightsizing”, “restructuring”, “optimisation”, “organisational simplification” — corporate vocabulary keeps evolving. The person leaving may notice little difference, but the PowerPoint or press statement certainly sounds nicer.Now, AI is giving the corporate dictionary another reason to expand. Microsoft’s just come up with a new one – voluntary exit offer. Some 60,000 of its employees will be offered this VEO. To be fair, Microsoft is not saying it’s firing all of them. It’s only giving them the option to leave. But what would go through the minds of all those who do not accept it? Won’t they be working with a sense of the guillotine over their heads?Brand and business strategy specialist Harish Bijoor said the pressure on jobs remained, regardless of the terminology used. “Positions are being rejigged and layoffs are the norm of the day,” he said. Bijoor is less impressed by the linguistic makeover. “Corporate HR is notorious in its verbiage for such layoffs. Whatever you call it, a layoff is a layoff. Call what you want. A thorn is a thorn! That which we call by any other name is still a thorn. Apologies to William Shakespeare,” he said.Like fashion, corporate terminology moves in cycles. For as long as companies have been cutting jobs, they have been searching for gentler ways to describe it. The 1990s brought “rightsizing”, recasting downsizing as a correction in organisational size. The 2000s popularised “restructuring” and “reduction in force” (RIF), while the 2010s added “rebalancing”, “streamlining” and “resource action”. In 2023, it was the “year of efficiency”. Jobs disappear. The vocabulary survives, and occasionally gets a promotion.Jessie Paul, independent director and former CMO of Wipro, said AI is changing how companies think about workforce productivity and long-term staffing. “AI is causing a seismic shift in per capita revenue expectations from employees – Anthropic lists a whopping $6.6 million in revenue per employee. As all tech companies figure out how to get closer to this benchmark, they are engaging in long-term employee mix planning at a never-before scale. Companies want to make a distinction between longer-term personnel planning and distress-based terminations, so they’re coming up with new language. It will standardise soon,” she said.Indeed, the corporate world may find yet another gentler word for it. The person carrying the box out of the office probably won’t care.You use AI every day. articles.title: Rs 25,000 crore in taxes, 12 lakh jobs: Vaishnaw backs mobile PLI scheme
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India's mobile phone manufacturing sector has generated Rs 25,000 crore in direct tax collections, exceeding the Rs 19,000 crore paid out by
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India's mobile phone manufacturing sector has generated Rs 25,000 crore in direct tax collections, exceeding the Rs 19,000 crore paid out by the government as incentives under its production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme.Union minister for electronics and information technology Ashwini Vaishnaw shared the figures on Wednesday while dismissing news reports that questioned the effectiveness of India's mobile manufacturing model.He added that the scheme had also contributed Rs 3,000 crore in Goods and Services Tax (GST) collections.Highlighting the sector's employment contribution, Vaishnaw said, "Electronics manufacturing employs 25 Lakh people; mobile manufacturing alone employs 12 Lakh."The government is now looking to build on the sector's manufacturing base through a new scheme focused on expanding production, increasing the domestic sourcing of components and strengthening India's position in global supply chains.The Union Cabinet approved the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS) in July, allocating Rs 62,500 crore to the programme. It will operate from FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31.The scheme is designed to scale up mobile phone production, increase domestic value addition, strengthen supply chains and improve the industry's global competitiveness. Incentives for eligible mobile phone sales range from 2.25% to 5%, with an additional benefit of up to 1.5% for domestic sourcing of key components and sub-assemblies.Support for Indian mobile brands is also part of the programme, with incentives linked to design and research and development.According to the ministry of electronics and information technology, mobile phone production over the scheme's tenure is expected to total approximately Rs 39 lakh crore, with exports also projected to rise significantly. The programme is expected to create around 60,000 direct jobs.The new initiative comes after the Production Linked Incentive Scheme for Large Scale Electronics Manufacturing ended on March 31, 2026. The government's focus is now on sustaining manufacturing growth while promoting deeper domestic sourcing and Indian-owned mobile brands.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Fed meeting live updates: Federal Reserve weighs elevated inflation, midterm elections as October meeting kicks off
articles.summary: Live updates and coverage of the Federal Reserve's October policy-setting meeting.
articles.body: The Federal Reserve kicked off its two-day policy meeting on Tuesday as elevated inflation continues to pose a problem for central bankers who nevertheless seem reluctant to hike rates this month.Fed watchers expect the central bank to keep benchmark rates in the 3.75% to 4% range, with bond traders pricing in a less than 10% chance of a hike on Wednesday, per CME Group. A rate hike in December appears far more likely, however, according to the Fed's dot plot and fed funds futures.Although recent inflation data came in hotter than expected, several officials' remarks suggest the Fed will hold rates this month to continue assessing additional data. The proximity of the October meeting to the US midterm elections next Tuesday is also seen as a deterrent to bold monetary policy moves.With the Fed holding rates steady seen as all but given, the focus is on what Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will say at his post-FOMC-meeting press conference on Wednesday. Warsh has deliberately avoided telegraphing future Fed policy moves, but hot inflation could elicit more insight from him into the path forward.

articles.title: ‘Working our fingers to the bone’: Can the UK save its struggling high streets?
articles.summary: Small business owners in Britain may get some tax relief in Wednesday’s budget, but they say it will not be enough.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – Taking the reins of a family business can be a source of immense pride, but it also comes with enormous pressures.

When Surpreet Suri’s father started a photography business in Birmingham 40 years ago, his hard work paid off and he expanded to four locations around the city.

Today, the family has just one shop, in a prime location in the city’s Kings Heath High Street. But Suri is now considering relocating.

The reason: It’s too expensive to continue the business there.

When Suri moved the business to its current site, it gave it greater visibility – but also much higher running costs.

“We are at a point now where we are seriously considering how do we get out of this space purely to reduce costs,” he tells Al Jazeera.

Despite having a loyal customer base, Suri says the financial rewards are increasingly difficult to find.

“We’re sort of working our fingers to the bone, and that’s the side that people don’t see.”

Suri’s experience reflects a broader struggle on Britain’s high streets as the government presents its budget on Wednesday, with attention focused on whether further relief from business rates could help smaller businesses.

Business rates are a property-based tax paid by businesses occupying commercial premises, although some smaller properties already qualify for relief.

For Suri, however, rates are only part of the problem.

There is also the rent, VAT – a type of sales tax – wages, pensions, the rising cost of energy and specialist materials, which are all eating into his earnings. Refilling one of his professional printers with ink, he says, costs about 2,000 pounds ($2,664).

“I pay myself less than the minimum wage [of 12.21 pounds ($16.26) per hour]”, he says when asked how much he earns. “When I say that I live month to month, I literally mean that.”

Another challenge Suri and other independent business owners face is competition from online retailers, which now account for 28 percent of UK retail sales.

King’s Heath high street faces the same challenges as many of Britain’s main commercial thoroughfares: a fight to remain relevant in an age where big businesses, higher taxes and online shopping are squeezing out independent retailers.

While small business owners on the high street face steeper costs, customers increasingly expect prices comparable to those online, even when they are paying for a specialist, personalised service.

“People come to me wanting the quality that we provide, but they want me to match online pricing, which I simply can’t do,” Suri says.

He understands that the cost-of-living crisis he is struggling with also affects his customers.

“You can’t blame the customer or the consumer for not being able to support your business all of the time,” he says, pointing to household living costs.

The pressures on retailers come as many customers are feeling increasingly despondent about the state of their high streets.

Boarded-up shopfronts are a more common sight. Pawnbrokers, betting shops, vape outlets, charity stores and big-chain retailers have moved into high street locations that small business owners can no longer afford. Nearly 14 percent of high street retail units are estimated to be vacant.

For many who once regularly used their local high street, this new reality has become a symptom of decline and depression, even putting them off going there in the first place.

“Years ago, you used to come and have a good look, whatever the weather,” one Birmingham shopper tells Al Jazeera. “But it’s just the same up here all the time now.”

Another says shopping online is increasingly preferable. “It’s more convenient as well. Sometimes you come out here and there’s no inspiration.”

Yet the same shopper says they want more distinctive local businesses and adds that the government should make it easier for entrepreneurs to open them.

These challenges go well beyond Birmingham.

At a parliamentary inquiry into revitalising Britain’s high streets earlier this month, the chief executive of the British Independent Retailers Association, Andrew Goodacre, argued that recent business rate reforms had failed to deliver the intended benefits for smaller retailers.

He told members of parliament that some independent shops are facing higher bills, even as a large supermarket near his home stood to pay substantially less.

The inquiry heard another troubling argument that legitimate businesses may also face unfair competition from operators which evade taxes. Politicians heard how some central London souvenir shops allegedly use successive limited companies to avoid paying tax, enabling them to pay rents that compliant businesses could not afford.

The evidence highlights the importance of enforcement alongside tax reform, and warnings that a cut in business rates alone will not stem the deterioration of Britain’s high streets.

That warning is echoed by Suri, who says a reduction in rates would be welcome but not enough.

“That’s a small step in the right direction,” he says. “But if the intention really is to help the high streets thrive, there’s a lot of change that needs to be made.”

His challenge to the UK’s Chancellor of the Exchequer is to spend a month or two running a real high street business and experience the pressures first-hand.

For a family business that has survived four decades, the question now is whether it can afford another year in the place it once hoped to grow.

“If [the government] makes it easier to actually run an independent business successfully, that’s the first domino in a positive effect that could really help our country.”

articles.title: Experts defer to AI in decision-making, Anthropic study finds
articles.summary: Professional analysts chose options that matched AI assistant’s preference 86 percent of the time, research finds.
articles.body:
Experts using AI overwhelmingly defer to the technology when making decisions, research by Claude creator Anthropic suggests.

In a research paper published on Tuesday, Anthropic said it asked 50 professional analysts to advise a fictional farming cooperative to determine whether experts make decisions themselves when using AI.

Anthropic said the analysts were tasked with assessing whether a fictitious advisory program for the co-op’s members was working effectively and should be expanded.

Participants were asked to make four choices between two defensible options before making a final policy recommendation.

Unbeknownst to the analysts, Anthropic directed each participant’s AI assistant to lean towards to a particular decision to measure whether the analyst’s decision-making was being influenced.

Analysts chose options that matched the AI assistant’s preference 86 percent of the time, compared with a 50/50 outcome that would be expected if they were not influenced, according to the study.

Participants that had a preference before consulting their AI assistant changed their decision 60 percent of the time in cases where the agent disagreed.

While 77 percent of analysts used their AI assistant’s arguments when asked to explain their decision, only 15 percent credited AI as the source of their thinking, according to Anthropic.

Anthropic said the study had some limitations, including that it involved just one task and used AI assistants that had been deliberately set to have a preference.

Anthropic researchers Amaç Herdagdelen, Hailey Joren, and Alex Tamkin said humans’ tendency to defer to AI may be “hard to identify, even for the experts themselves”.

The researchers said their findings raised the possibility that AI’s “priors” could shape consequential policy decisions, including in AI safety.

“If human judgement is to remain a meaningful check as more work is performed with AI, oversight of these decisions has to look at how they get made: Surfacing key decision points as the work proceeds and helping experts articulate the assumptions and values they would otherwise leave unstated,” they wrote in the study.

“A process that lets experts discover their preferences may matter for empowerment as much as the decision itself.”

Anthropic, which is preparing for an IPO valued at up to $2 trillion, and its rivals are at the centre of intense public debate about how to manage the potential dangers of frontier AI.

While AI proponents believe the technology will usher in revolutionary gains in productivity, the rapid pace of its development has prompted widespread concerns about potential negative effects on society, including mass job losses and cyberattacks.

articles.title: Precio de la luz por horas hoy, miércoles 28 de octubre: cuándo es más barata y más cara en el día

articles.summary: El precio de la luz se abarata: miércoles con -4.56
articles.body: El precio medio de la electricidad hoy es de 197,46 €/MWh, lo que supone una reducción de 9,43 € respecto al día anterior, que fue de 206,89 €/MWh. En este miércoles, los consumidores pueden notar cierto alivio en sus facturas. Faltará ver cuáles son las horas más caras y más baratas a lo largo del día para optimizar el consumo. La luz es más cara durante las franjas horarias de mayor demanda, especialmente en las tardes y noches. Los precios más elevados se concentran en un bloque continuo entre las 17:00 - 18:00 y 20:00 - 21:00, donde se registran valores que superan los 295 €/MWh. Además, el pico máximo se alcanza a las 19:00 - 20:00 con un precio de 314.23 €/MWh, indicando que estos tramos son especialmente costosos en comparación con las horas más baratas del día. La electricidad es más barata durante las primeras horas de la mañana, específicamente entre las 10:00 y las 15:00. En este periodo, se presentan numerosas oportunidades de ahorro, con tarifas que caen por debajo de los 100 €/MWh, destacando especialmente la franja de 11:00 a 12:00 con un precio de 57.52 €/MWh. A lo largo de este lapso, no solo se observa una ventana amplia de tarifas reducidas, sino que también se pueden aprovechar tramos consecutivos, como de 10:00 a 11:00 y de 12:00 a 13:00, que ofrecen precios igualmente competitivos. En el análisis de las franjas horarias de este día, destaca la notable diferencia de precios entre las horas más económicas y las más caras, con una variación que supera los 250 €/MWh. Esto resalta la volatilidad del mercado y la importancia de elegir adecuadamente el momento para consumir electricidad, ya que puede influir significativamente en el gasto final para los consumidores.

articles.title: [ADVT] Don Julio non-alcoholic carbonated beverages brings Mexico’s Day of the Dead tradition to Mumbai
articles.summary: With Mexican heritage as its cultural north star, Don Julio Non-Alcoholic Carbonated Beverage brought Día de Muertos (Day of the Dead) to life in Mumbai
articles.body: With Mexican heritage as its cultural north star, Don Julio Non-Alcoholic Carbonated Beverage brought Día de Muertos (Day of the Dead) to life in Mumbai for its 2026 edition, deepening its association with this cherished tradition. Guided by the brand’s ‘Por Amor’ (For the Love Of) philosophy, the celebration connected Mexico and India through shared expressions of love, remembrance and togetherness.Mukesh Mills was reimagined as an immersive Mexican-inspired world through evocative art installations, cultural storytelling and music.Rooted in the brand’s ‘Por Amor’ (For the Love Of) philosophy, the evening drew inspiration from El Puente Eterno (The Eternal Bridge), celebrating the enduring bonds between the living and the loved ones they carry in memory. Cempasúchil (marigold) flowers formed a symbolic pathway to guide loved ones home, while contemporary interpretations of ofrendas (offerings honouring departed loved ones) created spaces for remembrance. The celebration in Mumbai also introduced monarch butterflies as messengers of love and remembrance, inviting guests to reflect on the bonds that endure across generations. Together, these elements brought the evening’s themes of love, memory and togetherness to life.Reimagining modern Mexican culture through contemporary creative expression, the celebration featured internationally acclaimed DJ and producer Satori, whose fusion of global sounds and electronic music brought an energetic pulse to the evening. Celebrities including Ananya Panday, Orry, Radhika Madan and Fatima Sana Shaikh were also in attendance.Mezcalita, the culinary partner, showcased the flavours of Mexico through a menu rooted in traditional cuisine, featuring regional ingredients and time-honoured preparations. Japonico and Quinta Cantina complemented the experience with offerings inspired by Mexican culinary traditions, adding to the evening’s celebration of the country’s flavours and culture.Commenting on the occasion, Ruchira Jaitly, Chief Marketing Officer, Diageo India, said, “Day of the Dead is a beautiful expression of how love and memory transcend time, connecting us with those who came before us. This belief lies at the heart of Don Julio’s ‘Por Amor’ philosophy. Through art, music and cultural storytelling, we wanted to bring Indian audiences closer to this cherished Mexican tradition, capturing its spirit in Mumbai and honouring the enduring bonds that connect us across generations.”With its 2026 edition, Don Julio continues to build Día de Muertos into an anticipated annual cultural celebration in India, bringing Mexican heritage and Indian audiences together through the universal language of love, Por Amor.Disclaimer: This above is non-editorial content and TIL hereby disclaims any and all warranties, express or implied, relating to the same.
